1.hint: Think about what set *all* scalar multiples $t\vec v$ trace out geometrically, then write that as $\{\vec x : \ldots\}$.
1.caution: Remember: give the full set-builder description with "for some $t$," not just the line equation $y=2x$ alone.

2.hint: First check whether $\vec q$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec p$ before deciding what the span looks like.
2.caution: Don't assume two nonzero vectors always span all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ — check for a scalar-multiple (parallel) relationship first.

3.hint: Set up $\alpha\vec u+\beta\vec v=\vec w$ as a system in $\alpha,\beta$ and solve for both unknowns.
3.caution: After solving, plug $\alpha,\beta$ back into *both* coordinate equations — don't confirm membership using only one.

4.hint: Check whether $\alpha_1\vec a+\alpha_2\vec b+\alpha_3\vec c=\vec x$ is consistent for arbitrary $x,y,z$, not just plausible.
4.caution: Don't assume 3 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ automatically span $\mathbb{R}^3$ just from the matching dimension — actually verify the system is consistent.

5.hint: Find two points on the line, use their difference as the direction vector and either point as the shift.
5.caution: Use set addition, $\operatorname{span}\{\vec d\}+\{\vec p\}$, with $\vec p$ outside the span — the line doesn't pass through the origin, so it can't be written as one plain span.

6.hint: Pick three points on the plane, form two direction vectors from their differences, and pick one point as the shift.
6.caution: Verify your two direction vectors are non-parallel before finishing — three collinear points would silently collapse the "plane" into a line.

7.hint: Set $t\vec d+\vec p$ equal to the target vector and solve for a single $t$ that must work in every coordinate.
7.caution: Don't find $t$ from just one coordinate and declare membership — check that the same $t$ satisfies all coordinates.

8.hint: Solve $\alpha\vec v_1+\beta\vec v_2=\vec 0$ algebraically, or check directly whether one vector is a scalar multiple of the other.
8.caution: Don't assume two nonzero vectors must be independent — a scalar-multiple relationship between them is exactly what forces dependence.

9.hint: Row-reduce the homogeneous system $x\vec v_1+y\vec v_2+z\vec v_3=\vec 0$ and use any free variable to build an explicit solution.
9.caution: Don't stop at concluding "dependent" once a free variable appears — go back and write out the actual non-trivial combination equal to $\vec 0$.

10.hint: Look for a relation involving all three vectors together (e.g. try to write one as a combination of the other two), not just pairwise comparisons.
10.caution: Don't conclude independence just because no two of the three are scalar multiples of each other — with three or more vectors, dependence can come from all of them combined.

11.hint: Test each claim against the exact definitions of linear (in)dependence, and try small counterexamples involving $\vec 0$ where relevant.
11.caution: Don't stretch the two-vector "not a scalar multiple" test to sets of three or more, and remember $1\cdot\vec 0=\vec 0$ always makes $\vec 0$'s presence create a non-trivial relation.

12.hint: Check whether $\vec d_2$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec d_1$ before concluding the equation describes a plane.
12.caution: Don't assume direction vectors that "look different" numerically must be independent — always check for a scalar-multiple relationship first.

13.hint: Compare the number of unknowns to the number of equations in the corresponding homogeneous system to see if a free variable is guaranteed.
13.caution: Don't judge independence by whether vectors "look different" from each other — count equations versus unknowns in the homogeneous system instead, for any number of vectors exceeding the space's dimension.
